description:
ServerName::ip_address only takes &str. A caller who already has a std::net::IpAddr (from a parsed config), a [u8; 4] (from a TCP socket peer addr), or a [u8; 16] must:

  let s = ip_addr.to_string();
  let server_name = ServerName::ip_address(&s)?;

This is parse-then-stringify-then-reparse: 2 unnecessary allocations and 1 round-trip through textual normalization, all to land in the exact same internal [u8; 4] / [u8; 16] representation IpRepr already holds.

Missing constructors (all non-breaking to add later, but absence today is a defensive-code-forcing footgun):

  pub fn ip_v4(octets: [u8; 4]) -> Self
  pub fn ip_v6(octets: [u8; 16]) -> Self

And with std feature gate:

  #[cfg(feature = "std")]
  pub fn from_ip_addr(ip: std::net::IpAddr) -> Self
  #[cfg(feature = "std")]
  pub fn from_ipv4_addr(ip: std::net::Ipv4Addr) -> Self
  #[cfg(feature = "std")]
  pub fn from_ipv6_addr(ip: std::net::Ipv6Addr) -> Self

These are infallible (raw byte forms cannot fail validation — they always represent some IP address).

Caller impact: TLS server callers receiving SocketAddr::ip().octets() pay 2 alloc + ~µs CPU per request to round-trip through string form. For a TLS server doing 10k handshakes/sec this is measurable. For a no_std embedded caller doing it on every TLS handshake, the alloc may not even be available.

Severity P2: additive, non-breaking to add later. But pre-1.0 is the right time to settle on the IP-construction surface; otherwise the textual-only API will calcify in caller code.
title: No constructor from std::net::IpAddr / [u8; 4] / [u8; 16] — IP-bytes callers forced to stringify-and-reparse
